stimulus.text:
“We therefore beseech your Majesty, that your royal authority and influence may be graciously interposed to procure us relief from our afflicting fears and jealousies, occasioned by the system before-mentioned, and to settle peace through every part of our dominions, with all humility submitting to your Majesty’s wise consideration, whether it may not be expedient for facilitating those important purposes, that your Majesty be pleased to direct some mode, by which the united applications of your faithful Colonists to the throne, in presence of their Common Councils, may be improved into a happy and permanent reconciliation; and that in the mean time measures may be taken for preventing the further destruction of the lives of your Majesty’s subjects; and that such statutes as more immediately distress any of your Majesty’s Colonies may be repealed.”
—Olive Branch Petition, Second Continental Congress, July 5, 1775 (abridged)

books.section: Topic 3.5 The American Revolution, A. The War for Independence

stem: The petition shows that in July 1775 the Second Continental Congress still sought

options.text: The abolition of slavery in the colonies
options.misconception: The petition asks for repeal of distressing statutes and for peace; it says nothing about abolishing slavery.

options.text: Reconciliation with Britain inside the empire

options.misconception: Independence was declared a year later; in July 1775 Congress was still asking the king for reconciliation.
France did not ally with the United States until 1778, after Saratoga; in 1775 Congress was appealing to the king, not to France.

rationales.B: The petition calls the colonists faithful subjects, asks for a happy and permanent reconciliation, and seeks repeal of the harsh statutes.
rationales.C: Independence came in July 1776; a year earlier Congress was still trying to settle the dispute inside the empire.
rationales.D: The French alliance came in 1778; in 1775 Congress looked to the king, not to a foreign ally.
rationales.A: The petition says nothing about slavery; its asks are peace, reconciliation, and repeal of distressing laws.
rationales.general:
1. Hear how Congress addresses the king. It calls itself his faithful subjects and asks for his gracious help.
2. Hear what it asks for. Reconciliation, peace, and repeal of the harsh statutes — not independence or a foreign ally.
3. Place it in time. July 1775 is months after Lexington, and a full year before the Declaration.
Remember: a petition that calls the writer faithful and asks for peace is a bid to stay, not a bid to leave.
